Done. Here's what I found and built.

## The core finding: the model isn't ignoring the rules — it can't see the counter

I read all four v6b RICH traces step-by-step. The three nulls die identically, and the models **say it themselves**:

- `rich_4079`: *"Wait, `get_status` says 28/28 used. I have 0 left."*
- `rich_4070`: *"I'm out of tool calls! I must submit now. **But I haven't made any edits!**"*

Critically, **both had already localized correctly before dying.** rich_4079 reached `TableDataElement`/`on_text` in `markdown.py` — which *is* the gold patch's file — and diagnosed the mechanism correctly at call 31 with zero budget left.

Against `HARNESS_README.md` §6.2, two tools are free (`count_tool_call=False`):

| tool | counts against budget? | returns |
|---|---|---|
| `submit_patch()` | **No — free** | works even at 0 calls remaining |
| `get_status()` | **No — free** | `tool_calls_remaining`, `patch_size` |

**The v6b prompt mentions `get_status` exactly0 times.** I verified this in the shipped artifact. So the agent never knew a free budget oracle existed, couldn't see its own remaining budget, and only learned the limit when the harness killed it — at which point editing was already impossible.

This reframes the log's "commitment wall." It isn't unwillingness. The "MAX 3-4 locate calls" instruction was **unenforceable as written** — nothing let the model observe whether it was honoring it. Your instinct that it "won't listen" is right in effect, wrong in mechanism.

Notably, [line 6343](Gemma/GEMMA_EXPERIMENT_LOG.md) of the log already proposed free-`get_status` enforcement as option C. It was never built.

## What I built — [submit_v6c/](Gemma/submit_v6c/)

Three coupled prompt additions, all in the budget family:

1. **Budget oracle** — teach that `get_status()` is free and returns `tool_calls_remaining`; call it early and at decision points.
2. **Commit-by-remaining** — replace the unenforceable vibe with a checkable trigger: ≤14 left → stop searching, edit; ≤7 → apply smallest fix and submit; ≤3 → emit immediately. Plus the explicit correction: *"When you are out of locating budget you are still allowed to edit."*
3. **Bank as you go** — apply each item the moment it's located (targets rich_4070's 10-symbols-traced-0-edits).

**RICH-only gate, 6 tasks:** rich_4077 (anchor, must not regress), **rich_4079 (primary target — cleanest isolation of commit-timing from localization)**, rich_4076, plus three never-attempted EASY tasks. rich_4070 excluded as genuine difficulty, not commitment.

**Pre-registered bar:** rich_4079 flips to resolved with `patch_chars > 0`, rich_4077 doesn't regress, **and** traces show a `get_status` call before call 10 — because a flip without the mechanism is luck, not signal at n=6.

Kept everything measured-good from v6b: the 0.18 recipe, `edit_file` removed, single-agent, and `read_file` **exposed** (v21 dropping it made reads cost *more*).

Validation: 5/5 cells pass the `ast.parse` gate, all six task IDs verified present in `tasks.jsonl`, and the v22 landmines (`len(adapters)`, `enforce_eager`) confirmed absent. Full pre-registration written to the [experiment log](Gemma/GEMMA_EXPERIMENT_LOG.md).

One caveat worth flagging: this does **not** fix rich_4076's wrong-file problem — banking an edit earlier on a mis-localized guess may just submit the wrong edit faster. I stated that in the log rather than paper over it.

To run it: `kaggle kernels push -p .` from `submit_v6c/`. The v6 @ 0.12 and v6b kernels are untouched.

## The one-line answer

We spent 22 versions optimizing **submit_patch**, which the harness never required.

## Join #1 — the big one

`HARNESS_README.md` §8.1 states it plainly: if an agent exhausts tool calls or times out **without ever calling `submit_patch()`**, the harness still runs `git diff` and scores the result. Both 0.18 kernels tell the model this outright: *"the working tree is graded as it is, so an edit made in time counts even if you never reach `submit_patch`."*

This reframes every number in the log. v6b's nulls all reported `patch_chars=0` — but that doesn't mean "never submitted," it means **the working tree was clean**. No edit was ever written. We've been conflating:

| what the log calls it | what it is |
|---|---|
| "search-death / never committed" | no edit ever written |
| "never reached submit_patch" | **irrelevant** |

Our prompt has spent the whole project teaching the wrong objective. The right bar is "a source file must be modified before the wall." That's also the exact thing my v6c budget-oracle rule was groping toward — I diagnosed the blindness correctly but landed on `submit_patch` as the thing to teach, when the harness had already told us it doesn't matter.

## Join #2 — we cut a tool all four competitors keep

| kernel | tools |
|---|---|
| starter / lavinwins / verra | all 9, **incl. `edit_file`** |
| honghanh | 6, still **keeps `edit_file`** |
| **our v6b/v6c** | **7 — `edit_file` removed** |

We removed it based on **one task's trace**. And `HARNESS_README` §10.1 names that exact symptom's real cause: a large `edit_file` hitting `max_output_tokens` truncates the `<|tool_call>` tag. Documented fix = control `thinking_budget`/`max_output`, **keep the tool**. We instead inherited a heredoc that must be byte-exact — a harder problem.

## Join #3 — we called the graph tools our "strongest lever." They're the ones honghanh hard-bansLog line ~4721, from the v10 forensics:
> `search_similar_code: 0 | get_code_neighbors: 0 | get_code_subgraph: 0` — **"THE STRONGEST LEVER WE'VE FOUND"**

for tool in FORBIDDEN_TOOLS:

**Same measurement, opposite conclusion.** The tools return nothing because they demand exact fully-qualified IDs and rich's problem statements are 2-word PR titles. ## What the scale dial actually gives us

The tool is already built and does exactly what's needed:

- **effective scale = `lora_alpha / r`**, and `--scale S` rewrites alpha to hit `S ×` the trained strength
- **`--scale 0` is a guaranteed no-op** — any adapter can be neutralized without retraining
- **`--rank K`** truncates to a smaller adapter from the same run
- Config-only, CPU, no retrain

Our three adapters:

| adapter | r | alpha | eff. scale | trained on | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `adapter_dataset` | 32 | 64 | **2.0** | 23 rich edit-discipline | v19-LORA 1/5, edit_fail ↑ |
| `adapter_v2_dataset` | 32 | 64 | **2.0** | 46 all-repo | v2 gate 1/5 null |
| `adapter_v2_s05` | 32 | 32 | **1.0** | same weights, halved | never gated |

**Every one was served at effective scale 2.0 or 1.0 — never below.** All three trained to loss 0.26–0.43 on 23–48 examples. That's the overfit signature the log flagged, and the dial that dials it back has never been swept on the 31B.

## Why this is the right first move for RICH specifically

The documented rich failure is `edit_fail` — and the log's own verdict on it is *"a WEIGHTS limit, not a prompt-fixable one."* That is precisely the symptom a badly-over-applied adapter produces: the model fires edit calls confidently but can't reproduce the anchor.

The log already said it: *"if reduced strength stops regressing v10's wins, over-application was a big part of it. **No retrain.**"*

So the discriminating test is cheap and sharp:

| scale | hypothesis |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | current — over-applied, breaks things |
| **0.5** | **the prediction: edit_fail drops, wins return** |
| 0.25 | if 0.5 is too weak, the capability is gone entirely |

**Scale 0 is the control nobody has run** — it's v19's prompt with the adapter proven inert. If 0.5 beats both 1.0 and 0.0, the adapter carries real signal that's simply being over-driven.

`make_variant.py` is CPU-only safetensors surgery. Generating 0.5 / 0.25 / 0.0 variants is **minutes**, and each needs one free gate run (~32 min) unless bundled.

### 1. Robust File-Reading & Line-Range Assertions

- **The Problem:** The logs show multiple instances where the model called `read_file` with specific line ranges (e.g., `start_line=1652`), but the tool returned the beginning of the file instead or truncated output, forcing agents to fall back to `run_command` with `sed`.
- **The Improvement:**

- Patch the underlying `read_file` tool implementation to strictly validate and honor line boundaries (`start_line` / `end_line`), or return clear line-indexed structures.
- Alternatively, standardize entirely on robust snippet extraction helpers or pattern-based grep/view functions to prevent wasted tool calls and parsing confusion.

### 2. Automated Patch Verification Guardrails

- **The Problem:** Agents frequently burn precious tool calls on manual, repetitive scratch script creation (`cat > /tmp/repro.py`, running python, checking output) before submitting patches.
- **The Improvement:**

- Build a lightweight, automatic pre-submission validation hook or "Dry Run" utility that executes the target test file or checks syntax validity immediately before `submit_patch` is allowed.
- This prevents zero-byte submissions caused by budget exhaustion right at the finish line (as seen in `rich_4079` and `rich_4076`).

### 3. Dynamic Budget Allocation & Early-Stopping Heuristics

- **The Problem:** While the prompt injects strict guidelines ("COMMIT-BY-REMAINING", "tool_calls_remaining <= 14"), models occasionally get stuck down rabbit holes during search phases, hitting the 28-call hard limit with `patch_size = 0`.
- **The Improvement:**

- Implement an active circuit breaker in the agent runner framework. If an agent executes more than $N$ read/grep operations without an intervening `edit_file` call, force a system prompt injection or automatic intervention warning: *"Search budget half-exhausted; switch to editing immediately."*

### 4. Better Handling of ANSI/Regex and Escaped Strings

- **The Problem:** Tasks involving complex tokenizers or ANSI escape sequences (`rich_3278`) lead to fragile regex adjustments and trial-and-error debugging loops.
- **The Improvement:**

- Provide specialized parsing utilities or helper test scaffolds inside the prompt workspace for common libraries (like regex character class expansion rules or token stream slicing) to reduce syntax iteration overhead.

The reasoning: the board serves **W4A16**, and `HARNESS_README` says that's a serving-only format with **no quantized forward/backward path**. You cannot run LoRA gradients on it. So "train through the quantization" means training on the unquantized twin and serving across the gap — which is **what every adapter already does.** It's not a separate lever; it's the status quo.

What *is* available: train E2B/E4B **with their own quantization** as a proof-of-mechanism on small models, then see if the behaviour transfers. That's a research question, not a submission lever, and it needs hours we may not have.

## Honest revised position

| lever | feasibility |
|---|---|
| MLP targeting | **already done, refuted** |
| quantization-matched | **not a lever** — the gap is unavoidable |
| rank/data more | possible, needs a training run, ~2h+ |
| **q/v at scale 0.5** | **running now** |
| SKILL.md | feasible, never built, interface-only |
| tool ordering | feasible, trivial, untested |

So of the nine I floated, **three are already dead and one is running.** That's what checking feasibility first surfaces — and it's why your instinct was better than my list.

If you want something genuinely new tonight, **SKILL.md** is the only one neither the log nor any competitor has built. Want me to spec it, or wait on the scale sweep?

The relationship **runs backwards.** Tasks with the *most* docstrings in the trace have essentially *zero* retries; tasks with fewest have the most.

### Some training tasks can't be solved from the task text alone
Was going through my agent's failures on the public tasks and noticed something.

Out of 43 failed tasks, 12 failed because the hidden tests check for something the task description never mentions. The agent's fix was reasonable, it just couldn't have known the exact name or wording.

Two flavours:

1. Tests need a specific name (8 tasks)

- fastapi_15661: task says "Automate release preparation". Test does `from scripts.prepare_release import ...`. My agent made scripts/release.py. Import fails, done.
- fastapi_15280: the whole task text is "Add support for [@app.vibe](https://www.kaggle.com/app.vibe)()". Test calls it with a `prompt=` argument that is never mentioned.
- fastapi_15785: test checks for a class called `RouteContext`. That name isn't in the task.

1. Tests need exact wording (4 tasks)

- fastapi_14479: task says "improve the error message". Test wants exactly "Query parameter 'q' must be one of the supported types". My agent wrote "Query param 'q' must be of one of the supported types". Same behaviour, fails anyway.
Makes sense why it happens: the real fix and the tests were written together, so they match. The agent only gets the description.

This is from one run on the public training tasks, so I can't say how much of this is in the hidden test set. Curious if others see the same, and whether the test set was filtered for this.

## What that means for a LoRA

**Not by teaching the answer — by teaching the search strategy.**

A LoRA can't know `RouteContext` is the right name from weights alone. But it *could* learn the durable behavior:

> *"When the issue names no symbol, find the nearest sibling implementation in this repo and match its naming convention exactly."*

That's a **transferable strategy**, not memorized answers — which is exactly what survives the fact that the scored set is **different repos** than the public practice set. An adapter that memorized fastapi's names would be worthless on the hidden repos. One that learned "search for the sibling, copy its convention" transfers.

**Critical distinction:** this is the *only* LoRA target all evening that isn't closed. The failure mode we're actually fighting is `edit_fail` — the model can't reproduce an exact string. Conventional naming is exactly the signal that predicts which string.

## USER  [2026-10-14T01:44:53.058Z]

New Gemma 4 Models Available: 12B, E4B, and E2B
Hi everyone,

We've added support for several smaller Gemma 4 variants. You can now use any of the following models for your agents:

gemma-4-31b-it-qat-w4a16-ct
gemma-4-12b-it-qat-w4a16-ct
gemma-4-e4b-it-qat-w4a16-ct
gemma-4-e2b-it-qat-w4a16-ct
We don't support mixing variants within a submission, however. Every agent and subagent in your submission must use the same variant (though they can attach different LoRA adapters.)

These smaller models open up some new strategies:

More test time compute: Inference is faster and memory burden lower so you can execute more and longer reasoning turns and iteration cycles. You could also experiment with using ParallelAgent for concurrent LLM calls (though tool calls are still executed sequentially).
Faster and more accessible LoRA finetuning: Experiment with different setups more quickly and on more accessible GPUs. We provide L4x4s for use in interactive notebooks, but adapters can now be finetuned on a wider variety of consumer hardware.
More specialized agents: Smaller models use smaller LoRA adapters, so you can include more of them in your submission.
We're excited to see what you build!

## It explicitly detects our "serialization wall"

The harness recognizes three termination conditions and injects a targeted nudge:

| detected | what it says |
|---|---|
| **unclosed `<\|tool_call>` tag** | *"reached the token limit **before the tool call finished closing**. Do NOT repeat your prior reasoning — emit your next tool call immediately, and **split the change into smaller incremental edits**"* |
| `finish_reason` = LENGTH | *"reached the token limit while thinking"* |
| normal stop | *"Please continue your work..."* |

And it terminates when `consecutive_nudges > 3`.

**Read that against our traces:** rich_4070 *"I am literally typing the arguments wrong"* ×3 → gave up. rich_3882 *"I am not providing `old_string`"* ×3 → gave up. armA rich_3882: **52 identical retries**.

**That isn't an unwilling model. It's nudge exhaustion.** We've been trying to fix it with prompt text for 20 versions.

### ASSISTANT  [2026-10-15T02:34:37.226Z]

The zip is the whole submission, and the notebook never runs against the defects. The zip is a declarative agent config: `agent.yaml`, the prompt, the sampling and eval YAMLs, and optional LoRA adapters. It contains no code. Kaggle's scorer, the `swegemma` harness, does the rest. This is from [HARNESS_README.md](C:/Users/Biges/OneDrive/Documents/Desktop/kAGGLE/Gemma/comp_official/HARNESS_README.md), section 4. I haven't seen Kaggle's backend itself.

1. **Load:** it validates the zip, serves the one allowed base model (Gemma 31B QAT) with vLLM on its own GPUs (the README says 4x L4), and compiles the YAML into an ADK agent. No competitor Python is ever executed.
2. **Per defect:** each task gets a sandbox with the repo at the base commit. The agent loops with its 9 tools under your `eval_config.yaml` budget (28 calls, 8 min) until `submit_patch`, then the harness extracts the git diff.
3. **Verify:** a fresh container gets the patch plus the hidden test patch and runs pytest. Exit code 0 counts as resolved, and the score is the resolution rate.

- **The notebook only builds the zip.** The 0.22 kernel runs for 23 s with no model, and the zip it outputs is what gets scored.
- **Our own uploads confirm this.** We submit with `kaggle competitions submit -f submission.zip`, with no notebook at all, and those got scored too (v6w = 0.15).
- **That answers your Input question.** The notebook's inputs can't matter, so only the zip bytes do. The three differences I found (thinking 4096, the prompt, the agent name) plus noise are everything that could explain 0.22 vs 0.15.

**Caveats:**
- The number of tasks behind the public score, versus the hidden set used for final ranking, is still unverified.
- We can't run the real 31B locally, so the 12B gates are only a weak proxy and the board is the only real measurement.

I read the log end-to-end on the LoRA question. Here's the honest picture, and it changes the answer.

## The 31B LoRA ledger is closed as tried

Eight levers measured, all negative:

| lever | result |
|---|---|
| edit-anchor LoRA (q/v, r32) | edit_fail **worse** |
| all-linear incl. MLP (r32, 410 modules) | 0/5 "OVERBAKED", then 1/5 at alpha 0.5 |
| q/v at serve-scale 0.25 | **0/3**, 2 of 3 banked *nothing* (no-adapter: 3/3) |
| serve-time scale dial | exhausted, negative |
| MLP targets | refuted |
| quantization-matched training | impossible on 31B (w4a16 is serving-only, no grad path) |
| E2B/E4B adapters | fewer patches than their own base |
| sub-agents | refuted twice |

Our one LoRA submission scored **0.05** — the worst number we've ever recorded. So: do not retrain the same thing. That's a re-run of a refuted lever.

## But the *reason* they failed is not "LoRA doesn't work"

Every failure has a diagnosed, non-LoRA cause:

- **Capacity mismatch.** The v2 adapter pushed **46 training examples into 410 target modules at r=32** (934 MB). The 12B specialist died of over-strength: r=16/alpha=32 to loss 0.30 on ~32 examples → greedy decode collapsed into a repetition sink (all args → `1`), triggered by per-turn token-cap overflow. The log's own words: *"an ALPHA/SCALE problem first, a DATA problem second."*
- **Wrong target, twice.** Localization was prompt-solved at v17. Edit-anchors are a non-problem — the harness auto-unescapes `\n` and the 3-tier matcher forgave the one real anchor miss (1 of 17 edit calls, self-corrected).
- **Fake trajectories.** `edit_discipline_rich.jsonl` is 46 rows of 3-step cheat: read one slice → edit → submit, with the target file *handed to the model in the assistant turn*. Zero exploration, zero test-running, zero recovery. That shape is exactly what produced search-death on 3/5 tasks.

## What I'd train, if we train

**Target: WRONG-FIX.** It's 56/149 traced rich rows (37.6%) — the dominant class, ahead of RESOLVED 45, LOCATE 29, FOUND-NOT-LANDED 19. The model reaches the right region and writes a patch that fails the hidden tests. That's a correctness failure prompting provably cannot reach, and it's the only dominant class a LoRA can address.

**The data idea nobody has built:** we have 56 WRONG-FIX rows *with traces showing the exact wrong patch the model submitted*, and the gold patch for every one of those tasks. That's an automatic **contrastive set** — (our wrong patch → gold patch) on the same context. Far higher signal per example than plain gold imitation, and it aims straight at the measured dominant class.

**Shape, from the measured overfit:**
- q/v only, **r=8–16**, `alpha/r ≤ 1` (collapse at a/r=2, partial recovery at 0.5)
- **1 epoch**, capacity matched to ~100–200 examples — not 410 modules
- **early-stop on a behavioral metric, not loss.** Loss 0.30 was the overfit signal nobody acted on
- r=16 q/v ≈ 84 MB (localizer_v1's shape — it trained cleanly *and* loaded cleanly in scoring)

**Base: 31B, not 12B.** A 12B-trained adapter **cannot** serve on the scored 31B — dim mismatch, architecturally incompatible. And 12B serving measured 0/4 vs 31B's 1/4, 38% slower per task. 31B QLoRA trains free on Kaggle 4xL4 (96 GB, 30 GPU-hrs/week) — the rig is not the blocker.

## The actual blocker is data, and that's what to build this week

Our ceiling today: 46 anti-leak-verified rich rows (3-step shape), 103 localization rows (wrong target), 322 fastapi idiom rows (wrong repo), and **only 6 distinct rich tasks we have ever resolved** (3278, 3471, 3676, 3882, 4077, 4079). Six tasks is a memorization set, not a training set.

So the work while waiting is: extend `build_edit_discipline_data.py` to emit **real multi-step rich trajectories** across all 48 rich tasks (locate → read → reproduce → edit → run the failing test → submit), keeping the anti-leak verification, plus the WRONG-FIX contrastive pairs from our own traces. Target 100–200 rows.

**Pre-registered bar:** paired baseline/change gate on the 6 known-resolvable tasks (floor-guaranteed — base resolves them, so any adapter that drops them is caught immediately) plus the 3 hard ones (4076/4079/3469). Must resolve ≥ base on both sets with **zero argument-collapse and zero malformed keys**, with the malformed-key rate *opportunity-conditioned* (per read_file call, not a vacuous absolute zero — that was the refute pass's correction).

**Falsifier:** if a correctly-shaped, correctly-targeted 31B adapter still degrades patch generation, the LoRA path is genuinely dead and we stop spending on it.

One caveat I won't paper over: the log claims the 12B route "closes the quantization gap," but that's asserted, not verified — and since a 12B adapter can't serve on 31B anyway, I'd treat 12B as a dead end for submission and keep training on 31B.

### ASSISTANT  [2026-10-15T14:21:52.611Z]

Read the rules text rather than inferring. Short answer: **the structure is legal, but two things are hard-blocked, and one line is forbidden.**

## What's explicitly allowed

A macro/micro router is a first-class citizen of this harness:

- **Sub-agents with their own tool subsets** — `sub_agents/*.yaml` each declare their own `tools:` list. The starter kit does exactly this: root has 9 tools, `code_analyzer.yaml` has 4 read-only ones. `max_sub_agent_depth` is 50.
- **`AgentTool` delegation** — `agent_tool: {config_path: ..., skip_summarization: true}` lets the root invoke a sub-agent as a tool, keeping intermediate output out of its context. This is the documented context-isolation pattern.
- **Different LoRA adapters per agent** — `adapter: main_lora` on the root, `adapter: tool_lora` on the analyzer. So a *trained* router adapter is legal.
- **Different generation configs per agent** — each agent YAML has its own `generate_content_config`. Sub-agent A can run `thinking_budget: 4096 / temperature: 0.2`, sub-agent B `thinking_budget: 0 / temperature: 0.0`. All schema fields are permitted.
- **Workflow agents** — Sequential/Parallel/Loop (`max_iterations` 1..500) for control flow.
- **Skills with `.py`** — `.py` is an allowed extension for "ADK skill scripts", 50 MiB per skill, up to 1,000 skills, invoked via `run_skill_script`. Sandboxed runtime Python is allowed even though Python *entrypoints* are not.

So "a model that reads the issue and picks a path" = the root agent choosing which sub-agent to call. Fully legal.

## The two hard blocks

**1. Nothing can rewrite tools or numbers at runtime.** HARNESS_README L154, verbatim:

> Execution-altering ADK fields that bypass the sandbox (`tools`, `system_instruction`, `http_options`, `safety_settings`, or `response_schema` inside `generate_content_config`) are excluded from `GenerateContentConfig` by schema design and **will raise a validation error if set**.

So a model that emits "set my max_tool_calls to 40" gets a schema rejection, not a config change. Routing must be expressed as **static YAML structure the root selects among** — the root picks the sub-agent; it cannot mutate any agent's tools or sampling on the fly.

**2. The eval budgets are global and fixed.** `eval_config.yaml` is a single root-level `evaluation:` block (`timeout_seconds`, `max_tool_calls`, `max_time_minutes`, `max_turns`) — one set for the whole submission, not per-task, not per-agent, not runtime-editable. The harness does inject a `budget_warning` at `tool_calls >= 20` with `remaining <= 10`, so the model can *adapt its behavior* to pressure, but the numbers are not its to change.

**And you cannot ship your own base model.** `validate_single_declared_model` traverses the root plus every `sub_agents[*].config_path` and every `tools[*].agent_tool.config_path`; one variant per submission, every agent and sub-agent must match. "Training our own macro model" has to mean a **LoRA adapter on one of the four legal bases** (31b/12b/e4b/e2b qat) — not a custom model. Hard caps: <3 GiB total unpacked including adapters, `max_lora_rank ≤ 128`; the README's sizing table puts ~8 adapters at r=16.

## The forbidden line

From our own priors brief (E), which matters more than the technical rules here:

> **No problem-statement fingerprints.** Do not build or ship a `fingerprint(problem_statement) → gold_diff` map or any mechanism that recognizes a task from its problem-statement text / repo name / file tree and emits a memorized answer.
> **No task-id / dev-answer conditioning.** The public tasks are training FUEL (structure → generalizable priors, metadata STRIPPED at inference), NOT answers to submit.

A router that classifies *issue shape* (single-file vs multi-file, has-repro vs no-repro, fastapi-contract vs rich-render) and picks a path is legitimate. The moment it recognizes *this specific issue* and emits a memorized diff, it's the forbidden bake — and it would inflate the public split while collapsing on private rescoring, since there's no provenance check.

## My honest read on whether it's worth building

The **tool-subset half** has real measured motivation. We measured `read_file` line-range args malformed in 44/928 calls, and the log's own R3 fix is "route all READS through `run_command sed -n 'A,Bp'`". A sub-agent whose tool list *omits* `read_file` entirely is the legal, structural expression of a fix we've already measured — the model can't mis-use a tool it doesn't have.

The **numeric-config half is measured-dead.** The budget audit is explicit: v2 raised 25→40 calls and went 1/6 → 0/6 by pushing tasks into the *time* wall, with rich_4079 and rich_4076 among the timeouts. Verdict: "Budget is not the lever, up or down. Dead." A router that gives hard issues more budget would reproduce that regression; one that gives easy issues less budget buys throughput, and the LB scores resolution rate, not speed.

And the **multi-agent structure itself has failed for us twice** — sub-agents refuted in the dmitrii sweep and our own v8 regression, plus a known ADK bug. Meanwhile the dominant measured failure is WRONG-FIX at 34/56 contrastive records: well-formed edits on the right file with wrong content. A config router doesn't touch that.

So: legal, yes — and the restricted-tool-subagent version is the one piece I'd actually test, because it's the only half with a measured mechanism behind it. Want me to spec that as a paired gate against the current D prompt?

## Why it regressed — five measured failure modes

**1. The shared budget pool. This is the killer, and it's structural.** From the wheel-source verification (L5353-5356):

> ONE `SwegemmaContext` per task, ONE `tool_calls_used` counter, ONE `budget.tool_calls`. `create_tools()` binds that single budget to ALL agents. SequentialAgent/AgentTool are stock ADK wrappers → find-phase and fix-phase SHARE ONE POOL. **There is NO per-sub-agent budget.**

Measured damage across four versions: rich_4079 (v3) — the analyzer burned all 15 shared calls on grep quoting errors and returned garbage; rich_4076 (v8) — analyzer burned ~15 of 22 shared calls, main agent hit BudgetExceeded, **0-char patch**; rich_4076 (v14) — the sub-agent *found* the fix (`ListItem new_line=False`) but spent the budget getting there, so no edit ever landed.

That last one is the whole tragedy: the sub-agent did its job and still cost us the task.

**2. Never-compact sessions → overflow → empty patch.** AgentTool sessions never compact; 3 of 5 losses in one arm were sub-agent context overflows. And the overflow failure is nasty — `prompt_tokens + max_output_tokens > 32,768` → vLLM HTTP 400 → "Sandbox execution error" → **empty patch, discarding an earlier `submit_patch`**. ~1 task in 12 lost this way.

**3. No invocation discipline.** L3285: `code_analyzer` was wired as an `agent_tool` but `system.md` never said *when* to use it — unused dead weight costing context.

**4. dmitrii's independent sweep** confirmed multi-agent (sub_agents/analyzer/ParallelAgent/reconciler) did not beat single-agent.

**5. v17 was the sophisticated attempt and it worked — for the wrong problem.** SequentialAgent localizer→fixer with a clean phase boundary and handoff. Result: 1/5, "localization SOLVED," and the wall moved to `edit_file` tool-call formatting. The architecture did its job; localization just wasn't the bottleneck.

## The one shape we never tried

Every sub-agent we ever built **had tools** — 4 to 5 read/graph tools each. That's precisely what made them budget sinks.

The agent schema has three fields we have never used:

- **`include_contents: "none"`** — the sub-agent gets a fresh context with no conversation history. Directly attacks failure mode 2.
- **`output_key`** — writes its final text into `session.state` for the parent to read.
- **`generate_content_config` per agent** — including `max_output_tokens`, a *hard* cap on its output. This is the "HARD-cap the sub-agent's output" fix from L1091, and it's available.

So: **a zero-tool, fresh-context, hard-output-capped reviewer.** `tools: []` means it *cannot* drain the tool-call pool — failure mode 1 is structurally avoided rather than mitigated. Fresh context means it can't accumulate toward overflow. Hard `max_output_tokens` bounds its cost.

| | code_analyzer (v3–v8, v14) | v17 localizer | zero-tool reviewer |
|---|---|---|---|
| tools | 4–5 read/graph | 4 read | **0** |
| tool-call budget | drains shared pool | drains shared pool | **cannot drain** |
| context | default, never compacts | default | **`include_contents: none`** |
| output cap | none | soft, via prompt | **hard `max_output_tokens`** |
| job | localize (solved at v17) | localize (solved) | **judge a diff before submit** |

And the job is aimed at the measured dominant failure: **WRONG-FIX, 34/56** — well-formed edits on the right file with wrong content. A fresh-context second opinion on the diff is the one thing that targets that class.

- If most are near-misses that only running the hidden tests can distinguish, the reviewer is dead on arrival — and we skip ~70 minutes of GPU entirely.

That's the "don't eat all our time" answer: the cheap test can kill the idea, and it uses data that already exists.

Same 6-task gate we just ran for D (rich_4077, 4079, 4076, 3471, 3278, 3882), paired baseline/change, on Kaggle L4x4 at ~35 min per arm.

Good news: **your logprob numbers actually confirm that your LoRA adapters are loaded and active in the forward pass**, and the scoring environment uses the exact same patched vLLM 0.19.1 wheelhouse.

Here is why replacing `lora_A` and `lora_B` in `sample_submission` with $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$ (or even $\mathcal{N}(0, 100)$) only changes the top-1 logprob from `-7.4e-06` to `-3.7e-05` without changing the greedy text:

### 1. Why `-7.4e-06` vs `-3.7e-05` vs `-2.3e-05` is a ~1.6-unit raw logit shift (not numerical noise)
At `temperature=0`, vLLM greedy decoding is bit-for-bit deterministic (`0` difference across runs when weights are unchanged). The reason the shift looks like `~1e-5` on the top token `"2"` is **softmax saturation**:

- `logprobs` returns $\ln \text{softmax}(z)_1$, not the raw logit $z_1$.
- When $p_1 \approx 1 - 7.4\times 10^{-6} = 0.9999926$, the logit margin between `"2"` and the runner-up token is $z_1 - z_2 \approx -\ln(7.4\times 10^{-6}) = \mathbf{11.81}$.
- With `main_lora` ($\ln p_1 = -3.7\times 10^{-5}$), the logit margin drops to $-\ln(3.7\times 10^{-5}) = \mathbf{10.20}$ — a **1.61-unit shift in the raw logits** (and a **5×** change in $1 - p_1$).
- With `tool_lora` ($\ln p_1 = -2.3\times 10^{-5}$), the logit margin shifts to $\mathbf{10.68}$ (**1.13 raw logit units**).
- Because $\frac{\partial \ln p_1}{\partial z_1} = 1 - p_1 \approx 10^{-5}$ when $p_1 \approx 1$, an $O(1)$ shift in raw logits looks like $O(10^{-5})$ on the top-1 logprob, while the runner-up token logprobs (`top_logprobs=5`) shift by the full ~1.1–1.6 nats.

### 2. Why large random weights in `sample_submission` don't blow up the output
`sample_submission/adapters/main_lora/adapter_config.json` is a minimal 1-layer smoke-test stub with `"layers_to_transform": [0]` and `"target_modules": ["q_proj", "o_proj"]` — it only contains weights for **Layer 0** out of **60 layers**.

Unlike Llama/Qwen (where `o_proj` is added directly to the residual stream, so multiplying Layer 0 `o_proj` by a large number explodes the residual stream), **Gemma 4 uses Sandwich-RMSNorm + Q-RMSNorm**:

1. Immediately after `qkv_proj`, `q` passes through per-head `self.q_norm` (`RMSNorm`).
2. Immediately after `o_proj`, the attention output passes through `self.post_attention_layernorm` (`RMSNorm`) **before** being added to `residual`: `python hidden_states = self.self_attn(positions=positions, hidden_states=hidden_states, **kwargs) hidden_states = self.post_attention_layernorm(hidden_states) hidden_states = hidden_states + residual`"

## What actually went wrong

Not a pip problem — a **mount** problem. The hardcoded wheelhouse path globbed **zero** wheels, `/tmp/wheelhouse` stayed empty, and pip was handed an empty requirement list. That error message ("You must give at least one requirement to install") tells you nothing about the cause.

So it's a transient/first-run dataset attach failure on the new slug, not a config difference.

## The fix

1. `_resolve_wheelhouse()` tries both known mount layouts, then falls back to an rglob for any `*.whl` under `/kaggle/input`.
2. If it still finds nothing, it **raises with the actual contents of `/kaggle/input`** and names the real suspect — instead of letting pip emit a meaningless error.
3. An explicit assert refuses to call pip with an empty requirement list — closing exactly the fault that killed v1.
4. Fail-fast asserts on `DATA_DIR` and `MODEL_PATH`, so a flaky mount aborts in seconds rather than after an 18GB model load.

I **tested** the resolver rather than just writing it — extracted it from the source and ran it against four simulated layouts:

|---|---|
| canonical known path (v6w's) | known-path, 41 wheels ✅ |
| alternate path, no `datasets/` segment | known-path, 41 wheels ✅ |
| wheelhouse at unexpected depth | rglob-fallback, 41 wheels ✅ |
| **directory present but empty (v1's fault)** | **detected as missing, raises cleanly** ✅ |

v2 is **QUEUED** and also carries the corrected budget comment, so the pushed artifact no longer asserts anything I've since disproved.

### ASSISTANT  [2026-10-17T19:22:38.113Z]

**12B v2 pushed.** That was my bug, and it was a good one to catch.

## What broke

```
NameError: name 'SAMPLE_IDS' is not defined
```

I placed `RUN_FINGERPRINT` right after `Loaded N tasks` in **cell 2**, but `SAMPLE_IDS` is only defined in **cell 4**, and `SAMPLE_TASKS` only after the `by_id` loop. The instrumentation referenced two names that don't exist yet at that point.

## The fix — split it

- **Cell 2** emits `RUN_FINGERPRINT(config)` with only what exists there: model, prompt/sampling/eval shas, prompt_chars, tools, `has_subagent` — plus the sub-agent assert.
- **Cell 4** appends `tasks_sha` + `n_tasks` after `SAMPLE_TASKS` is built, re-prints the full fingerprint, and writes `run_fingerprint.json`.
- Both halves are guarded, so a failure degrades to a message rather than a crash.

## Verified by execution, not inspection

I ran the blocks in true notebook order against a stubbed agent dir:

- **Step 1** (no `SAMPLE_IDS`/`SAMPLE_TASKS` in scope) → OK, no NameError, task fields correctly absent
- **Step 2** (both defined) → full fingerprint with `tasks_sha`, `n_tasks`, file written

**ORDERING VERIFIED.**

That test also caught a **second instance of the same bug** in my first fix: I'd anchored the deferred block after `SAMPLE_IDS = ...`, which is still *before* `SAMPLE_TASKS` exists. It only passed because my stub supplied `SAMPLE_TASKS`. Re-anchored after the sample-loaded print.

## Two things worth noting

The failure was **loud and early** — cell 2, before vLLM loaded — so it cost a queue slot and **zero GPU-hours**. That's the mount guard and syntax gate doing their job.

And the lesson: **verifying code parses is not verifying it runs at the right time.** Only executing the blocks in notebook order caught this. `cover_rich` — the template every future arm forks from — carries the fix too.

Still outstanding: the **repo push is staged but uncommitted** (355 added, 4 modified), waiting on approval I can't grant.

Good catch — and there's a concrete explanation. Let me verify it against the E4B log.

### ASSISTANT  [2026-10-17T19:46:55.785Z]

Now the numbers explain it — and confirm your instinct that something's odd.

| model | wheelhouse done | server started | **startup** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 31B | 95.5s | 776.8s | **681.2s** |
| E4B | 83.2s | 557.6s | **474.4s** |
| E2B | 65.1s | 425.0s | **360.0s** |
| **12B** | 78.3s | 432.0s | **353.7s** |

Startup is otherwise cleanly monotonic with size: 31B (681s) > E4B (474s) > E2B (360s).

**12B is the exception** — it starts marginally *faster* than E2B despite having ~3× the parameters, and 120s faster than the much smaller E4B.

## The likely reason

12B is the **only** model we've forced onto the native text-only architecture. The `hf-overrides` remap maps it to `Gemma4ForCausalLM`, which bypasses the multimodal path entirely.

That path costs real time, and we can see it directly in the v2 crash log — before the remap took effect, 12B was on the fallback and logged:

```
Encoder cache will be initialized with a budget of 2048 tokens,
and profiled with 8 image items of the maximum feature size.
```

So on the fallback vLLM profiles a vision encoder before serving. The remapped 12B skips that step; E4B and E2B don't have the remap, so they still pay it. That would make 12B faster than E4B despite being larger — and it's the same reason the 12B v2 run needed124s just to load weights before it crashed.

## Honest caveats

- **n=1 per arm.** A 120s gap on a single run each is not strong evidence.
- The comparison is **confounded with the remap** — I can't separate "12B is fast" from "the remap is fast" with one run apiece.
- The vLLM internals (`Resolved architecture`, `Encoder cache`) only appear in logs on **failure**, so I couldn't confirm the mechanism directly on the successful runs.

The clean test would be applying the same remap to E4B/E2B and seeing whether they also speed up — but that's a serving-side question, not the size question you actually asked.

Here are some details from a Ai live reviewer of our notebook running while the notebook is running ### Top-level summary
**Biggest blockers**

- **Data leakage risk** from preprocessing done before splitting.
- **Evaluation blind spots**: single-split metrics and no per-task error analysis.
- **Experiment friction**: manual cell edits, no lightweight tracking, and inconsistent seeds.
**Quick wins (apply in this order)**

1. Move all preprocessing into a train-only `Pipeline`.
2. Add a small, reproducible experiment log (CSV or `wandb` free tier).
3. Add per-task error breakdown and targeted augmentation for the failing task.

## 1 — Preprocessing and leakage (highest priority)
**What I saw**

- Several feature-engineering cells compute statistics (means, label encodings, target-based aggregations) on the full dataset before any train/val split.
- A global imputation step uses dataset-wide medians.
- A cell creates time-derived features without ensuring splits are time-aware.
**Why it matters**

- Using full-dataset statistics or target-adjacent aggregations leaks information into training and inflates validation metrics. That explains why you hit 9/10 easily but can’t push the last task.
**Exact fixes**

- **Encapsulate transforms in a **`sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`** or **`ColumnTransformer` and call `.fit()` only on training folds. Example pattern:

- `preproc = ColumnTransformer([...])`
- `clf = Pipeline([('preproc', preproc), ('model', model)])`
- Use `cross_val_score` or `GridSearchCV` on `clf`.
- **For target-based aggregations** (e.g., group means), compute them inside CV folds or use `TargetEncoder` implementations that accept `cv` or `min_samples_leaf` to reduce leakage.
- **Imputation**: fit `SimpleImputer` on training only; do not compute medians on full data.
- **Time features**: if problem is temporal, split by time (e.g., `TimeSeriesSplit`) and compute rolling features only from past windows.

## 2 — Validation strategy and metric fidelity
**What I saw**

- Single train/val split used for most experiments.
- Final metric reported is a single aggregate (e.g., accuracy or overall score) without per-task or per-class breakdown.
- Hyperparameter tuning done on the same split (no nested CV).
**Why it matters**

- Single split hides variance and overfits tuning to that split. The missing task may be a distributional or class-specific failure.
**Exact fixes**

- **Adopt nested CV** for hyperparameter tuning or at least use a holdout test set untouched by tuning.
- **Use stratified or task-aware splits**: `StratifiedKFold` for class imbalance; `GroupKFold` if multiple rows per entity; `TimeSeriesSplit` for temporal data.
- **Report per-task metrics** (precision/recall/F1 per label or per-task error) and confusion matrices. Add PR curves for imbalanced classes.
- **Add a small “final holdout” run**: after tuning, train on full train set and evaluate once on holdout to estimate real-world performance.

## 3 — The “9/10” plateau: targeted diagnosis
**What I saw**

- No focused error analysis for the single failing task.
- Augmentation and class-specific strategies are applied globally rather than targeted.
**Why it matters**

- The last task often fails due to a narrow distribution, label noise, or missing features that only affect that class.
**Exact fixes**

- **Create an error analysis notebook cell**:

- Filter validation examples where the model fails the task.
- Inspect feature distributions, timestamps, and raw inputs for those examples.
- **If label noise suspected**: sample 50–100 failed examples and manually verify labels; add label smoothing or noise-robust loss if noisy.
- **If class imbalance**: apply class-specific augmentation, focal loss, or oversampling only for that class.
- **If OOD inputs**: add a small OOD detector or simple heuristics (e.g., missing key fields) and treat them separately.

## 4 — Model training and hyperparameter practice
**What I saw**

- Default hyperparameters used for complex models; single-run results reported.
- No learning-rate schedule or early stopping in place for gradient-based models.
**Why it matters**

- Small hyperparameter and training-stability changes often unlock the last bit of performance.
**Exact fixes**

- **Run short, focused sweeps** for learning rate, weight decay, and batch size (Optuna or simple grid). Limit to 20–50 trials.
- **Use early stopping** with a patience of 5–10 epochs and checkpoint best weights.
- **Run 3 seeds** for top candidates and report mean ± std to ensure improvements are robust.

## 5 — Experiment tracking and reproducibility
**What I saw**

- Notebook relies on manual notes and cell outputs; no run logging.
- Hard-coded paths are present (you said they’re required by the competition).
**Why it matters**

- Without tracking, small changes can’t be reliably compared; you lose signal on what actually improved the 9th vs 10th task.
**Exact fixes**

- **Add minimal logging**: append a CSV row per run with timestamp, seed, hyperparams, validation metrics, and path to saved model. This is low friction and works on Kaggle.
- If you prefer a hosted tool, use `wandb` free tier or `mlflow` local.
- **Pin seeds** at the top and log them. Example:

- `seed = 42; np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)`

## 6 — Data pipeline performance and caching
**What I saw**

- Tokenization / heavy transforms re-run on every experiment cell.
- No caching of processed datasets.
**Why it matters**

- Slow iteration reduces the number of experiments you can run, slowing progress.
**Exact fixes**

- **Cache processed datasets** to `/kaggle/working/cache/` with a checksum of raw data and transform config.
- Use `joblib.Memory` or simple `pickle` dumps with a versioned filename.
- Only re-run expensive transforms when the checksum changes.

## 7 — Code hygiene and notebook structure
**What I saw**

- Long monolithic cells mixing data loading, preprocessing, and training.
- Some cells mutate global state (e.g., reassigning `df` in-place).
**Why it matters**

- Hard to reproduce and easy to introduce subtle bugs.
**Exact fixes**

- **Refactor into clear sections**: `00_config`, `01_load`, `02_preproc`, `03_features`, `04_train`, `05_eval`.
- Make transforms **pure functions** that accept and return dataframes rather than mutating globals.
- Add `assert` checks after each major step (shapes, null counts, unique label counts).

## 8 — Monitoring and robustness checks
**What I saw**

- No checks for distribution drift or OOD examples.
- No unit tests for critical transforms.
**Why it matters**

- The failing task could be caused by a subtle distribution shift or an edge-case transform bug.
**Exact fixes**

- Add a small “sanity checks” cell that:

- Compares train vs val feature means and flags >10% shifts.
- Checks for new categories in categorical features and logs them.
- Add a few unit tests (simple asserts) for transforms: e.g., `test_impute_no_nulls`, `test_encode_consistent_categories`.

### What these checks reveal that post‑hoc analysis misses

- **Transient instability**: single-run snapshots hide short-lived gradient explosions or bad batches that corrupt training.
- **Forgetting patterns**: repeated flips on the same samples point to label noise or underfitting of a subpopulation.
- **Per‑task calibration drift**: a task can have good accuracy but terrible calibration, causing downstream decision failures.
- **Feature leakage in preprocessing**: drift or sudden changes in derived features often indicate a transform computed on full data or a time window bug.
- **Brittle examples and edge clusters**: hard examples cluster by a few features; fixing or augmenting those clusters often unlocks the last task.

### Lightweight triage workflow to run automatically

1. **Every epoch**: write `metrics.json` with per‑task metrics and call `report_metrics`.
2. **Every validation**: save `val_hard_snapshot.parquet` (top 100 losses).
3. **If stall or overfit detected**: run automated error analysis on `val_hard_snapshot` to output top 3 differing features and one representative sample.
4. **If batch loss spike or grad norm alert**: pause training, dump the offending batch inputs to `bad_batch_debug.parquet` for inspection.
5. **Daily**: compute forgetting statistics across epochs and list top 50 repeatedly forgotten sample IDs for manual relabeling.

### Quick heuristics to act on alerts

- **Many forgetting events concentrated in a class** → add class‑specific augmentation or focal loss.
- **High feature drift on a derived feature** → recompute that feature inside fold pipelines or remove it.
- **Batch loss spikes with high grad norms** → reduce LR, add gradient clipping, inspect batch for corrupted values.
- **High calibration error on failing task** → temperature scaling or recalibration on a held-out set.
- **Hard examples with inconsistent labels** → sample for manual relabeling or apply label smoothing.

So the lookup misses, defaults to `0`, and the console prints **"exit 0"** when the real code was `1`. That's what made your output look self-contradictory. It's display-only — the agent never sees this string.

## Bug 2 (agent-facing, this is the expensive one): empty searches are reported as errors

The handler is `if rc == 0: ok else error`. But `grep` returns **exit 1 when it finds nothing** — which is a *normal, successful* search result. So the agent receives:

```
status: "error",  error_message: ""   (empty stderr)
```

The model is told the command **failed**, with no explanation, when in fact it worked correctly and the answer was "no matches." It cannot distinguish "search found nothing" from "the tool is broken," so it rephrases and searches again — precisely the flailing in your snippet: *"That's strange. Let me try searching for 'hashed'..."*

Measured across all local runs: **72 of 818 `run_command` calls (8.8%) are errors with no message at all.** Worst offenders: `rich_3006` (19), `rich_3938` (12), `rich_3130` (11).

This is the same mechanism as the "search death" class already in our log — it burns calls on a non-problem, and those calls aren't free.

The tool side is **not** shippable — the submission is YAML-only with a fixed tool list. So this can't be patched at the source.

> `run_command` reports a bare `error` with no output when a search finds nothing — `grep` exits 1 on no match. That is a SUCCESSFUL search with an empty result set, not a malfunction. Re-search with a different term; do not treat it as a broken tool.

That line is harmless — it's in **all 34** of our run logs, including every one that scored and resolved tasks normally. It's not your new kernels misbehaving.

## What it is

The competition's submission validator has an optional function, `validate_single_declared_model`, whose job is to enforce the rule **"this submission may declare exactly one model."** That guard ships in some wheelhouse builds but not the one mounted here (`metric/gemma-4-developer-agent-wheelhouse`, 41 wheels).

So the harness does what it should when a check is absent — **logs it and falls back to a no-op**:

```
[import] validate_single_declared_model NOT FOUND; using no-op (single-model rule satisfied by agent.yaml)
```

Read it as: *"I would have checked your model declaration; that checker isn't installed; I'm skipping it — and the rule it checks is already satisfied because your agent.yaml declares one model."*

## Why it's safe for us specifically

- Our `agent.yaml` declares **exactly one** `model:` line — so the rule holds by construction, not by the validator's blessing.
- The rule exists to stop people declaring multiple models and picking the best after seeing results. We're not doing that.
- Every prior run — including v6w at **0.15** and the 31B's 10/10 — carried the identical line.

**No action needed.** The `NOT FOUND` is informational, not a failure, and the `[import]` prefix confirms it's an import-time probe rather than an execution error.

**"A5 used fewer calls" is misleading.** Per-task it's **19 fewer, 20 more, 5 equal** — a coin flip. The aggregate advantage comes from A3's outliers (28 calls on `3063`) rather than A5 being systematically leaner. I reported the total without the distribution. That was a real omission.

### ASSISTANT  [2026-10-19T03:29:36.679Z]

Confirmed. **This is a genuine harness bug, and it explains A5's failure completely.**

## The bug

Two different ways of measuring the same patch:

```python
# get_status  (line 901) — NO git add -N
"patch_size": len(git(["diff", task["base_commit"]]).stdout)

# final_patch (line 220) — WITH git add -N
git(["add", "-N", "."])
return strip_protected(git(["diff", base_commit]).stdout)
```

`git diff <commit>` **does not show new/untracked files.** `submit_patch` runs `git add -N .` first, so it sees them. `get_status` doesn't.

## What happened to A5

```
392.3s  get_status → patch_size: 0        ← wrong; new files invisible
396.3s  "Wait, patch_size is 0. That means my edits didn't stick?"
398.3s  submit_patch → patch_size: 3772, files_changed: 5   ← correct
401.0s  "patch_size is 3772. So my changes were accepted! I'm done."
```

A5 had **5 files changed**. It edited `repr.py` *and* created new files. `get_status` reported **0** because the new files were untracked. A5 concluded its edits had failed, burned its last calls re-reading `repr.py` to verify, and submitted with **1.3 minutes and 2 calls left** — rushing a 3772-char patch instead of its clean fix.

The model **did the right thing** — it diagnosed the identity-check bug correctly. It was misled by a false "you have nothing" signal from the tool it trusted for budget state.

## Why this matters beyond this task

Our prompt tells the agent to call `get_status` constantly as the budget oracle. So the oracle **lies about patch state specifically when there are new files** — which is exactly when an agent is mid-way through a multi-file fix.

This likely explains a chunk of what we've been reading as "never committed": the agent is told the patch is empty, second-guesses itself, and churns.

## The fix

**Prompt-side (shippable, and the highest-value change we've found):**

> `get_status` reports `patch_size: 0` if you have CREATED any new file — it cannot see untracked files until you `submit_patch`. **Do not re-read or re-edit because of it.** Your edits are fine. Submit.

That single line would likely have saved A5's `rich_3006` run.

**Harness-side (not shippable, but worth logging):** `get_status` should run `git add -N .` before diffing, exactly as `final_patch` does.

Honest answer: **I don't know, and the mechanism matters less than whether it's real.** Let me lay out the candidates and the test.

## Four candidate mechanisms

1. **Tokenization.** `ONE` and `1` aren't the same tokens. Whether this matters is checkable — but it's a weak lever for behaviour.
2. **Emphasis convention.** Digits read differently from words in prompt text. `with 1 grep` looks like a *specification*; `with ONE grep` reads as prose emphasis. Models do treat numerals as more literal/structural.
3. **Numerical anchoring.** `1` is a smaller, more concrete quantity than `ONE`. If the model was reading "ONE" as "a few," `1` removes that latitude.
4. **Nothing.** The 7/9 vs 6/9 gap is one task.

| A3 | 6/9 | 178 | 2584s |
| A5 original | 5/9 | 177 | 2364s |

**Our prompt instructs this exact failure.** Line 53 says *"Scratch/repro files go to /tmp via run_command heredoc."* The model reaches for `write_file` first, gets blocked, and burns calls recovering.

```

It wrote a repro, it **didn't reproduce**, and the model concluded it might be wrong — *after* correctly identifying the cause twice. It then re-read the same ranges four more times, second-guessing a hypothesis it had already formed correctly.

```
- Scratch/repro files go to /tmp via run_command heredoc `cat > /tmp/x.py <<'EOF'`.

  `write_file` is sandboxed to the repo and REJECTS `/tmp` ("Path traversal detected").
  Never point `write_file` at `/tmp`.
```

Honest answer: **mostly yes — with one caveat worth keeping.**

## The numbers

| | |
|---|---|
| Prompt size | 7,528 chars |
| **Markup characters** | **95 (1.3%)** |
| Asterisk-bolds | 6 spans, 278 chars wrapped |
| Backtick-code spans | 34 spans |
| SHOUTING capitals | 97 words |

**Nothing renders.** The prompt arrives as plain text — `**get_status()` is FREE.**` reaches the model as literal asterisks. There's no markdown renderer in the tool-call path, so no glyph is ever bold.

## The caveat

There *is* a learned signal, just not a visual one. These are instruction-tuned models pretrained on enormous amounts of markdown, where `**` reliably marks importance. The model has likely seen millions of examples where asterisks mean "this bit matters."

So the asterisks aren't visual bold — they're a **learned delimiter that correlates with emphasis**. That's weaker than rendering, and much weaker than the model actually obeying the content.

## What the evidence supports

Our best arm — `all-`1`s`, 7/9 — changed `ONE` → **plain `1`** with no asterisks and won. So the one change we've measured as beneficial involved **removing** a word in favour of a bare numeral, not adding markup.

Everything else is untested decoration.

## The distinction I'd draw

| Markup | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `` `get_status()` `` backticks | **Keep.** These delimit *literal tool names* — they mark "this exact token" vs prose. That's semantic, not decorative. 34 spans, all identifiers. |
| `**...**` asterisks | **Probably inert.** 1.3% of prompt, no rendering, weak learned association. |
| 97 SHOUTING caps | **Unknown, probably inert.** Same argument. |

The backticks are doing real work — they're how the prompt says *this is the literal string you must emit*. That matters enormously for A3's delimiter fix, which is our one proven win and depends on the model reproducing `<|"|>` exactly.

## Recommendation

**Strip the asterisks, keep the backticks.** It's a ~12-character change, zero risk, and consistent with the only measured win we've had — which came from making instructions *more literal*, not more decorated.

But I want to be honest about the expected value: after five consecutive falsifications, I'd put this at **low confidence**. It's cheap enough to fold into the next arm rather than test alone, and I wouldn't ship it on the strength of the reasoning alone.

## Yes — and the math says we've been underpowered by ~10×

**Runs needed per arm** (80% power, α=0.05):

| Effect size | n per arm | Total | Local time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.50 → 0.60 | 384 | 768 | **21.5 h** |
| 0.50 → 0.55 | 1,560 | 3,120 | 3.4 days |
| 0.50 → 0.65 | 166 | 333 | 9 h |

**What we actually measured tonight:**

| Comparison | n per arm |
|---|---|
| A3 vs A5 (dur9) | 63 |
| A11 v2 @12B | 3 |
| A3 @31B hard | 5 |
| all-`1`s @12B | 9 |

We've been trying to resolve 10-point effects with **n=3 to n=63**. That's not a measurement — it's a coin flip with extra steps. Every "win" and every "falsification" tonight was underpowered.

## What 10k runs would actually give us

**1. Per-task solve probability with confidence intervals.** Not "A3 got 4/5" but "`rich_3454`: p=0.86 ± 0.09". That's the number that lets you compare arms.

**2. The tool-calls-to-solve distribution** — your specific question. For each task: minimum calls, median, p90. That answers:
- Is 28 the right budget, or would 14 lose nothing?
- Which tasks are call-bound vs time-bound vs never-land-an-edit?
- Does a prompt change reduce calls-to-solve, independent of whether it converts a task?

**3. The real noise floor**, measured rather than assumed.

## The blocker isn't API access — it's throughput

We already have the API (local vLLM). The ceiling is the **sequential agent loop**: each tool call depends on the previous, so you can't batch within a task. And E4B uses ~9GB of 16GB VRAM, so we can't run tasks concurrently either.

1.61 min/task is close to the hardware floor on one 5070 Ti.

## What I'd build

A batch runner that:
- Loops N reps × M tasks × K arms, unattended
- **Auto-restarts the server on death** — it failed twice tonight (BOM, then `reasoning_config`), and both times it silently produced garbage
- Writes per-run JSONL, then computes per-task p with Wilson intervals
- Flags degenerate runs (patch >8k) separately rather than letting them poison the aggregate

**800 runs ≈ 21.5 hours** would settle `ONE`→`1`, the `get_status` bound, and `freq_penalty` — the three questions we've been guessing at all night.

Want me to build it? It's the difference between another night of coin flips and actually knowing.

`pip install a.whl b.whl c.whl` treats the list as **one transaction** — if any wheel is incompatible, the whole thing can abort. Installing individually means each wheel succeeds or fails on its own, and you keep the 40 that fit.

## `run_guarded.py` — records the facts, not guesses

| Event | What it records | Distinguishes |
|---|---|---|
| `spawn` | PID, full command, server state at launch | — |
| `task` | task, resolved, **gap since last task**, **server up/down** | B vs C |
| `stall` | no-progress duration, last task, server state, proc alive | **A vs B** |
| `exit` | **exit code**, duration, **stderr tail** | **A** |

## How to attack `rich_3772`

**The key fact I found earlier: the test only needs a one-line guard.**

The test is `raise e from e`, which sets `e.__cause__ = e`. The loop in `extract()` does:

```python
cause = getattr(exc_value, "__cause__", None)
if cause:              # cause IS exc_value → always true
    exc_value = cause  # reassigns to itself
    continue           # infinite loop
```

**Minimal fix: `if cause is not None and cause is not exc_value:`**

The gold patch is 45 lines because it *also* fixes the second linked issue (3682, ExceptionGroup). But `test_recursive_exception` only exercises the self-reference case.

## What the model actually does

From the 31B trace: it found the loop, understood the recursion, then chose to **replace 140 lines with a stack-based rewrite**. That oversized edit blew the output budget and got truncated mid-`<|tool_call|>`.

From E4B: 5/59 resolves, so it *can* get there — p≈0.085.

## Three attack options, ranked

**1. A pattern-library entry (highest value, testable)**

Add to the prompt:

> **When traversing a linked chain** (`__cause__`, `__context__`, `next`, `parent`, `prev`), **check for self-reference before following it.** `raise e from e` sets `__cause__` to the exception itself; a loop that follows the chain without that check never terminates. The fix is usually one added condition, not a rewrite.

That's the v2 task-type pattern idea, but *specific* — it names the exact bug class. And it's the A3 category: giving the model a fact it doesn't have, not telling it to try harder.

**2. The granularity rule** — "change as few lines as possible; if one condition prevents the bug, change one line." Already tested in A11 v2 (0/3), but that arm had three other changes confounded in.

**3. A verify-and-retry loop** — generate a candidate, run the test, if it fails try again. The harness allows it, but it costs calls and the model already burns 28.

## Results

**P1 2/3 vs A3 0/3, Fisher exact p = 0.400. Not significant.** n=3 per arm. This is a direction, not a result — I'm not going to call it a win.

## The finding that *is* robust

A3's three failures were **2× SyntaxError + 1× timeout**:

- `while exc_value is not None` — **missing colon**, and 7 edit attempts with 0 landed
- duplicate `max_frames` kwarg
- pytest timed out

P1/P2's failures were timeouts — a *logic* failure, not a syntax failure. P1 and P2 had **zero edit errors** across all 6 runs; A3 had 7.

So A3 doesn't fail this task by picking the wrong fix. It fails by **emitting syntactically invalid Python and being unable to land an edit at all**. That's the same class as the A3 delimiter fix — a serialization/parsing mechanism, not a behaviour instruction.

## The winning mechanism

Cycle detection, and every resolve is 3–20× smaller than the 45-line gold patch:

- **P1_r1** (667 ch): `visited: Set[BaseException]` + `if exc_value in visited: break`
- **P1_r3** (1490 ch): `processed_exceptions` + `cause is not exc_value` on both `__cause__` and `__context__` — most complete
- **P2_r1** (729 ch): `processed_exceptions: set[int]` + `id()` tracking

## A data-integrity bug I had to fix first

`p3772_*.results.jsonl` are **append logs** — 9 of 12 files contain the same tag twice with *different* results. My first pass double-counted and reported A3 0/5, P1 2/5, P2 1/5, P3 1/6. All wrong.

I rebuilt from the last row per tag, cross-validated against the guard logs (one `task` event per invocation). They agree on calls/patch/first_edit/edit_err in every case. `A3_r3` and `P1_r4` have a guard `start` but no `task` event — killed mid-run.

## Two things I want to flag honestly

**The sweep was well-designed** — interleaved by rep, so each arm is balanced across the 1.5h window and server drift isn't confounded with arm. By rep: rep1 2/4, rep2 0/4, rep3 1/4. There *is* a time effect, but P1 won in both rep1 and rep3.

**The pattern arms were built for rich_3772.** A single-task win says nothing about whether P1 generalizes. The real test is P1 on the other 8 cohort tasks — and that's the only result that would justify adopting it.

My read: the syntax-error failure mode is the more valuable lead. A3 emits invalid Python on punctuation-heavy edits, which is mechanistically the same as the delimiter fix that already took us 0.15 → 0.18. That's worth a dedicated arm more than another pattern variant.

Built and tested: **`Gemma\local_eval\sweep.py`**

## What was actually wrong

`gate_run.py` already had `--skip-done` and `--max-time`. The sweep loop never used them — and neither caps the *total* sweep. So this is a driver, not a patch.

## Six guarantees

| # | Guarantee | Verified |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Resume** — rerun the identical command, completed runs skipped | ✅ |
| 2 | **Budget** — `--budget-min` stops *launching*; in-flight finishes or is killed, then clean exit | ✅ stopped with 2 runs left |
| 3 | **No dupes** — canonical atomic rewrite, one row per key | ✅ |
| 4 | **Hard cap** — child killed by a watchdog thread | ✅ |
| 5 | **Clean exit** — Ctrl+C finishes in-flight, flushes, exits 0 | logic-tested |
| 6 | **One sweep** — PID lock; stale/corrupt locks reclaimed | ✅ |

## Three real bugs found while testing

**a) The watchdog was in the wrong place.** My first version checked the timeout inside the `for line in proc.stdout` loop. That loop *blocks* on `readline()`, so the check never fires while the child is silent — exactly the hung case the cap exists for. A 30s child ran to completion against a 12s cap. Fixed with a timer thread; the same test now kills at 14.5s.

**b) Crash rows were marked done.** A run that produced no result row was written as done, so resume skipped it *forever* — a transient crash would permanently poison the sweep with a false negative. Now `driver_crash`/`killed_max_run` are retryable: still written for audit, never counted as done, dropped once a real result exists.

**c) Double task run.** `gate_run`'s `read_tasks` **concatenates** `--tasks` and `--tasks-file`. Passing both ran every task in the file on every run. Now only `--tasks` is passed — verified in the guard log.

Also fixed: a UTF-8 BOM in a tasks file (PowerShell's `Out-File -Encoding utf8` writes one) was becoming part of the first task ID, and non-ASCII output could crash a cp1252 console.

## Usage

```powershell
python sweep.py --name p3772 --reps 3 --budget-min 60 `
    --arms A3=prompts/e4b_A3_delim.md,P1=prompts/e4b_P1_chain.md `
    --tasks-file one3772.txt --repo-dir repos/rich `
    --model /home/biges/models/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-w4a16-ct `
    --thinking on --temp 0.2 --max-tool-calls 28 --max-time 480
```

**Resume after a crash: the identical command.** Narrow to missing work with `--arms P1`.

## One design change worth knowing

Jobs are interleaved **by rep** (`A3,P1 | A3,P1 | …`) so wall-clock drift is balanced across arms instead of confounded with them. The rich_3772 sweep did this by hand — it's now automatic, which matters because that sweep showed a real time effect (rep1 2/4, rep2 0/4, rep3 1/4).

For your next run I'd suggest `--budget-min 45 --max-run-min 10` — that caps the whole sweep at 45 minutes and any single hung run at 10, so a stall costs you 10 minutes instead of your PC.

Logged in [GEMMA_EXPERIMENT_LOG.md](Gemma/GEMMA_EXPERIMENT_LOG.md).

## 91 of 124 recorded patches are corrupted

They report 10–136 files and 10k–780k chars, full of deletions the model never made. Example: `v2_A3_r4/rich_3882.patch` is 307KB across 80 files — but the trace shows the model made **two** `edit_file` calls, both to `rich/prompt.py`, plus four greps.

**Proof it isn't model behaviour:**
1. A clean `git reset --hard <base>` + `git add -N .` + `git diff <base>` produces **0 chars** — I verified this directly.
2. `dur9_A3_r1/rich_2725` and `abl_E1_r1/rich_2725` are **byte-identical** (181,131 chars / 61 files). Independent runs can't do that.
3. Sidecar writes from different tags land **2–9 seconds apart**. Multiple `gate_run` processes were running concurrently against the same `repos/rich`.
4. Not cumulative — in `v2_A3_r4` sizes go 832/601/394 → 307,508/675,894 → 521/657/657/558. Two tasks blow up, the rest are clean.

**Diagnosis:** concurrent runs share one working tree; each one's `reset_repo` wipes the others' edits, and `git diff` captures the mixture. Same root cause as your PC crash.

**Honest limitation:** I could *not* reproduce the exact phantom diff in a minimal two-thread test. The corruption and the concurrency are both measured; the precise interleaving isn't pinned down.

## Fixed

- `gate_run.py --isolate` — each run gets its own git worktree (own tree/HEAD/index, shared object store, no disk cost). Verified it creates, populates, and removes cleanly.
- `sweep.py` passes `--isolate` **by default**.
- `gate_run.py` already had `--repo-dir` for exactly this — the sweeps just never used it.

## What this does to the numbers

- `rich_4077`'s 10/39 includes 12 corrupted runs. Its real rate is unknown.
- The "degenerate runs (patch >8k, excluded from p)" filter was excluding runs for a **harness** reason, not a model reason.
- Clean runs are still valid — `rich_3006=558`, `rich_2725=1099`, `rich_2943=400`. The patch-size fingerprint finding stands on those.

## Two more things that change the prompt plan

**22/124 runs (17.7%) are infra deaths** — `chat_error:HTTPError` at call 0–1 with `error=None`. `abl2_A3` and `abl2_E1` are **6/6 infra deaths, zero valid data**. Any conclusion from those arm families is void.

**And the failure mix, on clean data:** TEST_FAIL 61.2% | RESOLVED 22.3% | NO_PATCH 7.8% | **SYNTAX 4.9%** | TIMEOUT 3.9%.

That last number corrects what I told you earlier. I said the syntax-error mode was "the more interesting lead" — at ~5% of failures it isn't. The dominant failure is **wrong content**, and A3 already tells the model three times not to touch unrelated files (L26, L53, L54), so an "edit fewer files" arm would repeat an instruction that's already there.

## My recommendation

**Re-run the cohort with `--isolate` before designing any new arms.** The history audit also turned up two constraints worth respecting: A1 already tested syntax-prevention (failed, 24% compliance), and the rule is **substitute, never append** — A4 broke A3's win by adding length.

## Two bugs I hit and fixed getting here

**`GATE_SERVER=vllm` was never set.** `run_local.py` defaults `SERVER_KIND` to `"llama"`, so it was sending llama-server thinking params to a vLLM server. The model emitted tool calls as raw text and every run died as `nudges_exhausted` with `calls=0`. `sweep.py` now sets it in the child env.

**`sweep.py` never passed `--prompt-file`.** It parsed `--arms A3=prompts/e4b_A3_delim.md` into a dict and then never used it — so every "arm" was being measured against the *default* prompt. That's why runs showed `calls=1, patch=0`. With the prompt wired through: `calls=20, first_edit=15, patch=1060`. I added a guard that fails loudly if a prompt file is missing or if `--prompt-file` is passed manually.

## Connecting Google Drive to the IDE/CLI

Your constraint: ~8 GB of task data plus a 2.5 GB model, read-mostly, and only **49.6 GB free on C:**. So you want streaming, not syncing.

| Option | How | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **rclone** (recommended) | `winget install Rclone.Rclone`, then `rclone config` for OAuth, then `rclone mount gdrive: G: --vfs-cache-mode writes` | Streams on demand, no local copy, VS Code opens `G:\` like any folder |
| **Google Drive for Desktop** | Install, sign in, set to **"Stream files"** not "Mirror files" | Gives `G:\` automatically; Mirror mode would eat your free disk |
| **Drive API + Python** | `google-api-python-client` with OAuth | Most control, most setup; only worth it for scripted pulls |

rclone is the better fit here — it's a real filesystem mount, it handles the 2.5 GB model without a full download, and it works from both the IDE and the CLI.

## 2. The 129-run, in paper detail

Full report: [129_ANALYSIS.md](C:/Users/Biges/OneDrive/Documents/Desktop/kAGGLE/Gemma/129_ANALYSIS.md). Key findings:

**Headline:** 34/129 = **0.264** (Wilson 95% CI [0.195, 0.346]) vs board 0.18 (≈23/129). Wall 10.8 h — fits the 12 h cap (mean 302 s/task).

**By repo — the fastapi overturn:**

| repo | solved | rate |
|---|---|---|
| rich | 15/48 | 31.2% |
| **fastapi** | **18/67** | **26.9%** |
| requests | 1/13 | 7.7% |
| httpx | 0/1 | — |

The log's "Zero fastapi ever resolved" was a small-sample artifact of the v1–v8 era. **The score is not a rich-only game.**

**By fix shape — contract-shaped converts, additive doesn't:** string/message 3/3, single_token 3/5, signature 2/4 | add_raise 0/5, add_import 0/3, pure_deletion 0/3.

**Failure anatomy (95 misses):** 57 wrong content (60%), 27 no patch (28%), 11 call cap (12%). Of the 27 no-patch: 16 never submitted, 16 never edited, 11 edited but submitted empty.

**Compliance — three significant correlations** (Fisher, one run, associations not causation):

| behaviour | solve rate | vs complement | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| get_status called ≥1 | 36% | 15% | **0.009** |
| submitted exactly once | 32% | 7% | **0.008** |
| non-empty patch | 33% | 4% | **0.001** |

Against that: **47% never called the free status tool, 0/129 called it ≥3 times, 90% blew the 3–4-call locate limit, 21 never submitted, 7 submitted 2–10×** (requests_6757: ten times) despite explicit rules.

**Tool-level failures are zero on 31B:** edit_file 0 errors / 279 calls (exact 146, unescaped 38) — A3's delimiter fix is complete at this scale, versus 62% error on E4B. The 203 run_command "errors" are 202 benign `exit 0` flags. **After A3, everything that remains is decision-level.**

**Rich retention:** 15/16 prior solves kept; only rich_3471 lost (20 calls of locating, 0 edits — ignored A3's own sed advice).

**No deterioration:** patch size vs position r = −0.127, no OOM, no compaction, 2 token truncations.

**For the paper**, the strongest framing this supports: *instruction non-compliance at scale* — explicit rules exist, the model violates them 47–90% of the time, and compliance predicts success at p<0.01; combined with the E4B four-arm null (adding more rules doesn't help), the open lever is **rule salience, not rule count** — which is untested on 31B.
